narrative.title: Why this role, why now
narrative.body:
I spent the first part of my career in institutional finance, most recently at Goldman Sachs, managing 20+ institutional relationships across multi-million dollar syndicated loan portfolios in a competitive, team-based selling structure. The win was never mine alone. It depended on coordinating with internal partners and earning trust with senior stakeholders who had every other option available to them.

In 2025, I watched a stranger save someone's life during a medical emergency, and it pushed me to earn my EMT license. I finished in the top 5% of my cohort at UT Dallas. During clinicals I worked in the emergency department, on patient transfers, and in the ambulance, including supporting a physician through an emergency tracheotomy and coordinating an air transport intake from helipad arrival through trauma bay admission. I learned to stay composed and useful inside a matrixed clinical team under real pressure, and I came out of it able to hold my own in a clinical conversation.

I'll name the gap directly. I don't have three years of medical device industry experience, and I haven't worked ECLS cases. What I do have is the underlying work that requirement is built to screen for. As a full-time volunteer territory representative across Nebraska, Iowa, and South Dakota, I built a network of community advocates from nothing, including one influential leader everyone told me to write off. I spent months building a real relationship with his family before ever asking him for anything, and he eventually opened his entire network to me. That is what developing a skeptical advocate into an active one actually looks like, proven outside a traditional device sales seat.

I'm also bilingual in Spanish, which helps me build genuine rapport with the staff who often decide how much time a clinician has for a new conversation, and I'm comfortable working independently from a home office based territory model.

I live in the DFW metro and I'm ready to bring that same approach here: earn trust first, understand what the person in front of me actually needs, and keep showing up until the relationship converts.

startStories.title: Developing an Advocate From a Cold Start
startStories.teaser: The leader everyone told me to write off, and what it took to earn him back.
startStories.body: During my 18 months as a volunteer territory representative, each area had an appointed community leader who was essentially the gateway to an entire network of prospects. Mine hadn't worked with anyone from our group in years, and everyone before me said not to bother. Instead of pushing him directly, I built a relationship with his wife first, weekly lunches, genuine friendship, listening for what actually mattered to him. She mentioned he missed playing soccer with a group he'd lost touch with, so I organized a recurring game and told him all he had to do was show up. He did, and over time he went from ignoring us completely to opening his entire network to us. Resistance is usually just information about what someone actually values, and that is the same patience a hard to reach clinical advocate requires.

startStories.title: Team Selling Under Pressure
startStories.teaser: Why the win at Goldman never belonged to me alone.
startStories.body: At Goldman Sachs, I managed 20+ institutional relationships across multi-million dollar syndicated loan portfolios, completing 10 to 20 complex transactions a week with zero-defect accuracy in a 70+ hour workweek. When a senior client pushed back on a contract term, I found the misread myself, but closing it out meant getting internal leadership aligned before I ever went back to the client. The account was retained because the team moved together, not because I closed it solo, the same coordination a role built around Territory Managers and Business Development partners requires.

startStories.title: Staying Useful Inside a Clinical Team Under Pressure
startStories.teaser: What an emergency tracheotomy taught me about matrixed teams.
startStories.body: As an EMT, I worked directly in the emergency department, on patient transfers, and in the ambulance. I assisted an ER physician during a high-acuity emergency tracheotomy and supported an air transport intake from helipad arrival through trauma bay admission, executing under pressure alongside physicians, nurses, EMTs, firefighters, and trauma teams. I finished in the top 5% of my cohort and came out of it able to hold a real clinical conversation, and comfortable being one more coordinated piece inside a fast-moving, multidisciplinary team rather than the only person responsible for the outcome.

startStories.title: Call Planning & Territory Coverage
startStories.teaser: Deciding who gets called on, how often, and why.
startStories.body: Across a 3-state volunteer territory, I built a repeatable cadence of visits and referrals instead of relying on cold outreach, with individualized pre-call plan objectives and post-call evaluations tracked through a CRM pipeline. At 1-800 Contacts, I built a nationwide marketing heat map across 42,000+ U.S. ZIP codes to identify exactly where coverage should be concentrated for maximum reach, the same analytical backbone behind deciding who gets called on, and how often.

startStories.title: Turning Data Into an Executive Business Case
startStories.teaser: Sizing an opportunity, then getting the C-suite to fund it.
startStories.body: At Vivint, I diagnosed territory-level performance gaps and built executive forecasting models in SQL, Snowflake, and Python. I translated that analysis into a business case that secured a $2M+ revenue expansion opportunity directly from senior leadership, the same skill it takes to identify a new business opportunity in a territory and make the case for it clearly enough that someone with the authority to say yes actually does.

startStories.title: Mentoring While Hitting My Own Number
startStories.teaser: Onboarding a new teammate without missing a weekly target.
startStories.body: As a volunteer territory representative, I consistently met daily and weekly performance targets while onboarding and mentoring a new representative at the same time. At the BYU CASA chapter, I presided over a 5-person leadership team overseeing 100+ volunteer advocates, building trusted relationships with judges, attorneys, and families through emotionally intelligent communication. Both are the same coachability and team orientation this role asks for, staying accountable to a number while also making the people around me better.
